elements.id-string-28: The sustainable development of next-generation device technology is paramount in the face of climate change and the looming energy crisis.
elements.id-string-29: Tremendous efforts have been made in the discovery and design of nanomaterials that achieve \textit{device-level} sustainability, where high performance and low operational energy cost are prioritized.
elements.id-string-30: However, many of such materials are composed of elements that are under threat of depletion and pose elevated risks to the environment.
elements.id-string-31: The role of \textit{materials-level} sustainability in computational screening efforts remains an open question thus far.
elements.id-string-32: Here we develop a general van der Waals materials screening framework imbued with sustainability-motivated search criteria.
elements.id-string-33: Using ultrawide bandgap (UWBG) materials as a backdrop -- an emerging materials class with great prospects in dielectric, power electronics, and ultraviolet device applications, we demonstrate how this screening framework results in 25 sustainable UWBG layered materials comprising only of low-risks elements.
elements.id-string-34: Our findings constitute a critical first-step towards reinventing a more sustainable electronics landscape beyond silicon, with the framework established in this work serving as a harbinger of sustainable 2D materials discovery.
elements.id-string-36: Since the isolation of graphene in 2004 \citep{graphene_isolation}, two-dimensional (2D) layered materials have received immense interest due to the myriad of unusual physical properties they possess.
elements.id-string-37: Of significance to the development of next-generation nanoelectronics is the family of 2D semiconductors, including those derived from van der Waals (vdW) layered bulk parents, such as transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) \citep{2DTMDC}, and those synthetically derived, such as \ce{MA2Z4} \citep{MA2Z4_1,MA2Z4_2,MA2Z4_3}, Janus TMDCs \citep{janus_TMDC} and liquid-metal-printed ultrathin oxides \citep{2D_TeO2}.
elements.id-string-38: Because of their ultrathin bodies and excellent electrical properties \citep{2D_FET}, 2D semiconductors form an emerging materials platform to realize sub-10~\si{nm} gate length field-effect transistors (FETs) \citep{sub10_2DFETs} -- an otherwise challenging feat using conventional silicon-based device technology.
elements.id-string-39: Recent demonstrations of ultralow contact resistance below 100~\si{\Omega \mu m} \citep{cont_res_1, cont_res_2, cont_res_3}, steep-slope devices \citep{slope_1, slope_2, slope_3}, ultrascaled transistors \citep{ultrascale_1, ultrascale_2}, and chip-scale integration \citep{chip1, chip2, chip3} have cemented the prospects of 2D semiconductors as a building block in low-power, high-performance transistors \citep{2D_transistors_1, 2D_transistors_2} critical for sustainable computing electronics.
elements.id-string-40: These achievements are based largely on 2D semiconductors with moderate bandgaps, leaving the family of ultrawide bandgap (UWBG) semiconductors relatively unexplored.
elements.id-string-41: Conventional UWBG semiconductors, such as SiC and GaN, hold important roles in dielectric applications, power electronics and deep-ultraviolet photonics \citep{UWBG_review}.
elements.id-string-42: How 2D materials can be used to enhance the performance of UWBG semiconductor device technology remains an open question thus far.
elements.id-string-43: With the development of highly-parallel density functional theory software, modern supercomputing systems and large materials databases \citep{materials_project, materials_cloud, 2dmatpedia, c2db1, c2db2}, computational screening has become an effective strategy in accelerating materials discovery and design.
elements.id-string-44: Previous 2D materials screening efforts have covered diverse functions ranging from photocathode coatings \citep{ht_1} and thermoelectrics \citep{ht_2} to piezoelectrics \citep{ht_3} and ferroelectrics \citep{ht_4}, even leading to experimental realization in the case of the layered piezoelectric \ce{NbOI2} proposed in Reference \onlinecite{ht_3}.
elements.id-string-45: While functionality and material stability form the main thrusts of these screening efforts, sustainability concerns are often neglected.
elements.id-string-46: Even when the notion of sustainability is invoked, it refers to \emph{device-level} features rather than \emph{materials-level} sustainability.
elements.id-string-47: Take for example the recently proposed UWBG layered dielectrics \ce{Bi2SeO5}, an experimentally synthesized native oxide related to high-mobility \ce{Bi2O2Se} \citep{Bi2SeO5_1, Bi2SeO5_2}, and \ce{LaOCl}, the result of a dielectric screening effort \citep{2d_dielectric_screen}.
elements.id-string-48: Their high dielectric constants ($\kappa$) and low leakage currents make them excellent gate dielectric materials capable of reducing power wastage and optimizing device efficiency, thus improving the sustainability of FETs at the \textit{device level}.
elements.id-string-49: Their comprising elements, however, are prone to supply risks and pose risks to the environment and human health because (i) the known reserves of \ce{Bi} and \ce{Se} are expected to be depleted within 50 years \citep{sus_chemsuschem}; and (ii) \ce{La} is a rare Earth element whose mining has adversely impacted the environment and human health \citep{rare_earth_elements}.
elements.id-string-50: Ostensibly, the inclusion of stringent element-based sustainability and safety criteria could significantly diminish the pool of high-performing candidates screened for a specific application.
elements.id-string-51: These considerations lead to the central questions of this work: How sizable would the pool of sustainable UWBG 2D semiconductors be, and to what extent can these candidates meet specific (opto)electronic device requirements given the imposition of such selective sustainability-focused screening filters?
elements.id-string-52: In this work, we screen the 2DMatPedia \citep{2dmatpedia} database for likely synthesizable UWBG 2D semiconductors composed of low-risk elements that may improve the sustainability of 2D semiconductor device technology at the `upstream' materials level.
elements.id-string-53: The sustainability-focused screening strategy introduced in this work filters out elements that pose elevated risks to the environment and human health, and are themselves prone to supply risks.
elements.id-string-54: The candidates are subsequently characterized with ab initio calculations, largely based on density functional theory (DFT), and assessed for their performance in various applications.
elements.id-string-55: Despite the stringent sustainability-motivated search criteria, we identify multiple candidates with promising performance as (i) high-$\kappa$ gate dielectrics compatible with low standby power operation; (ii) low-$\kappa$ spacer materials with good mechanical strength; (iii) broadband deep ultraviolet (UV) photodetectors and polarizers.
elements.id-string-56: Using ab initio quantum transport simulations, we further demonstrate that \ce{CuI}, one of the screened candidates, can function as a channel material in sub-10~\si{nm} FETs to fulfill the operation requirements of the International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors (ITRS) \citep{ITRS}, even at elevated temperatures up to 600~\si{K}.
elements.id-string-57: These results highlight \ce{CuI}'s potential in computing electronics capable of high-temperature operations, typically required in electric vehicle (EV) and space exploration applications.
elements.id-string-58: Our findings constitute a critical first-step towards reinventing a more sustainable electronics landscape beyond silicon.
elements.id-string-59: This work provides a radically different perspective on 2D materials screening with the introduction of sustainability-motivated search criteria.
elements.id-string-60: The framework established here shall serve as a harbinger of sustainable 2D materials discovery, and can be generalized to the screening of other classes of sustainable 2D functional materials.
elements.id-string-62: Screening Procedure and Summary of Candidates
elements.id-string-63: In this section, we first introduce a broadly applicable sustainability-focused 2D materials screening framework that can also be tailored for other applications.
elements.id-string-64: We then discuss how this framework is employed to catalogue sustainable 2D UWBG semiconductors that are well suited for dielectric, transistor and UV optical device applications.
elements.id-string-65: Our screening procedure is based on three guiding principles - \textit{functionality} (ultrawide bandgap), \textit{sustainability and safety}, as well as \textit{synthesizability and stability}.
elements.id-string-66: An overview of the screening procedure and the calculations performed in this work is presented in Figure~\ref{overview}a.
elements.id-string-68: The key functional attribute considered in this work is an ultrawide bandgap, which we define as a gap exceeding 3~\si{eV} \citep{2d_wide_gap}.
elements.id-string-69: As 2DMatPedia only provides PBE gaps, well-known to underestimate experimentally measured bandgaps, we screened for PBE gaps exceeding 2~\si{eV}, which are expected to map onto more accurate HSE06 gaps above 3~\si{eV} \citep{monolayer_bandgap_benchmark}.
elements.id-string-71: The aim of this filter is to select materials composed of low-risk elements based on the following risk factors.
elements.id-string-73: The periodic tables of `endangered elements' from References~\onlinecite{sus_pnas}, \onlinecite{sus_chemsuschem}, \onlinecite{sus_euchemsoc} and \onlinecite{sus_acs} were analyzed and combined to form an element-based filter for excluding candidate structures whose constituting elements are under serious supply risk (more details are presented in the Supplementary Information).
elements.id-string-75: We excluded environmentally damaging elements identified in the criticality study of Reference~\onlinecite{sus_pnas}, which found that gold and platinum group noble metals were the most harmful due to their extraction and processing methods.
elements.id-string-76: The rare Earth elements, including all 15 lanthanides, \ce{Y} and \ce{Sc}, are also excluded due to the environmental harm associated with mining them \citep{rare_earth_elements}.
elements.id-string-78: We additionally exclude elements known to be carcinogenic, namely \ce{As}, \ce{Be}, \ce{Cd}, \ce{Ni} and \ce{Cr}, as they can form complexes that catalyze redox reactions that cause DNA oxidation \citep{element_cancer}.
elements.id-string-79: The periodic table highlighting these risk factors is shown in Figure~\ref{overview}b.
elements.id-string-81: To improve the likelihood of synthesizing the screened candidate materials, we only consider monolayers that are likely to be exfoliated from already experimentally found bulk parents.
elements.id-string-82: Methodologically, this translates to only considering the `top-down' structures from 2DMatPedia, that is, the ones theoretically exfoliated from their bulk parents in the Materials Project database \citep{materials_project}.
elements.id-string-83: We further require the bulk parents to have an experimental record based on Material Project's matching algorithm to entries in the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database (ICSD), and lie within 10~\si{meV}/atom of their convex hulls in Materials Project.
elements.id-string-84: Additionally, an upper bound of 100 \si{meV}/atom was imposed for the exfoliation energies provided by 2DMatPedia to increase the likelihood of exfoliation.
elements.id-string-85: As for stability, we only select structures with decomposition energies below 100~\si{meV}/atom since 53 experimentally grown structures found in 2DMatPedia fulfil this requirement \citep{2dmatpedia}.

elements.id-string-93: As outlined in Figure~\ref{overview}a, we first applied the \textit{ultrawide bandgap} criteria to the 2,940 `top-down' structures from 2DMatPedia, yielding an initial group of 934 candidates.
elements.id-string-94: Further application of the \textit{sustainability and safety} filter on these 934 candidates results in a significantly shrunk pool of 253 candidates.
elements.id-string-95: The \textit{synthesizability and stability} filter further reduces the number of candidates to 48.
elements.id-string-96: This remaining pool is then pruned for non-vdW entries (those without clear vdW layers and/or with substantial dangling bonds) through manual inspection of their bulk structures.
elements.id-string-97: Candidates with more than 25 atoms in the monolayer unit cell are also removed due to their complexity and high computational cost.
elements.id-string-98: This results in 30 shortlisted candidates, just 1\% of the initial pool of 2,940 `top-down' 2DMatPedia entries, highlighting the rather stringent nature of this screening framework.

elements.id-string-143: The insulating property of UWBG materials makes them viable for dielectric applications.
elements.id-string-144: Here we consider the potential roles of 2D UWBG in transistor applications as (i) high-$\kappa$ gate dielectrics, and (ii) low-$\kappa$ spacers.
elements.id-string-145: To assess the dielectric performance of the 2D UWBG candidates, their dielectric constants are computed, postprocessed \citep{hBN_dc_dft, 2d_dielectric_screen}, and summarized in Figure~\ref{dielectric}.
elements.id-string-146: We make the following general remarks on the dielectric properties of the UWBG candidates.(i) The electronic contributions to both in-plane and out-of-plane dielectric constants are largely comparable going from the layered bulk to the monolayer limit.
elements.id-string-147: The large difference in total dielectric constant between the bulk and monolayer for certain candidates, therefore, can be attributed predominantly to the ionic contribution.
elements.id-string-148: (ii) In terms of in-plane components, \ce{S(IO3)2} possesses the largest dielectric response, ranging from 30 to 35 for its bulk form and up to 50 in its monolayer form.
elements.id-string-149: (iii) More pertinent for gate dielectric applications, the monolayer candidates with the largest out-of-plane dielectric constants are \ce{NaNbCl6} (15.3), \ce{KHCO3} (9.8) and \ce{BaH4O3} (8.3).
elements.id-string-150: (iv) As the ionic parts of the dielectric constants are significantly larger in some candidates' monolayer forms than in their bulk forms, it is necessary to check if they originate, erroneously, as artefacts from using an insufficiently thick vacuum layer in the DFT simulation cell.

elements.id-string-175: We estimate the leakage currents based on the Tsu-Esaki formalism \citep{tsu_esaki} implemented in Comphy \citep{comphy_1, comphy_2}, though we note that other tunneling equations, such as the Fowler-Nordheim and Richardson-Dushmann laws, can also be used for the modelling of gate leakage current \citep{2d_dielectric_screen, TMNH_dielectric, hydroxides, vandenberghe_review}.

elements.id-string-177: For ultrathin vdW materials, however, more care is required in estimating vertical tunneling masses since the vertical effective mass of the layered bulk arises due to the out-of-plane crystal periodicity, a feature that is completely absent in few-layer vdW materials.
elements.id-string-178: Experimentally, recent work by \citet{tunneling_mass} has demonstrated a peculiar layer-dependent tunneling effective mass for \ce{WSe2} (extracted by fitting the Fowler-Nordheim tunneling equation to their transfer curves).
elements.id-string-179: Particularly, the extracted tunneling effective mass of monolayer \ce{WSe2} of 3$m_e$ deviates significantly from the bulk effective mass of 0.2-0.3$m_e$ \citep{tunneling_mass}.

elements.id-string-181: In view of this, we treat $m^\text{diel}_\text{tun}$ as an empirical fitting parameter and consider a range of relative tunneling effective masses (0.5, 1 and 2) in this work.
